items.prompt: During which months does the Northern Hemisphere receive the most direct sunlight?

options.label: November, December, and January
options.feedback: Wrong. That is when the Southern Hemisphere faces the Sun most directly.

options.label: May, June, and July
options.feedback: Correct. The Northern Hemisphere faces the Sun during these months, giving it the most direct sunlight.

options.label: March, April, and May
options.feedback: Wrong. The tilt peaks around late June, so spring months have less direct sunlight than summer.

options.label: September, October, and November
options.feedback: Wrong. The tilt peaks around late December for the Southern Hemisphere, not in early autumn.

items.ok_line: May through July are the brightest for the north.
items.ko_line: The most direct sunlight comes when the hemisphere tips toward the Sun.
items.exp_text: Earth's tilt makes the Northern Hemisphere lean toward the Sun from around March to September, with the strongest lean near June 21. That is why May, June, and July get the most direct sunlight there.

items.prompt: How many seasons do many tropical regions typically have?

options.label: Four
options.feedback: Wrong. Four seasons are common in temperate and sub-polar regions, not in many tropical areas.

options.label: One
options.feedback: Wrong. Tropical regions usually have more than one season, often two or sometimes three.

options.label: Two
options.feedback: Correct. Many tropical regions have a rainy (wet or monsoon) season and a dry season.

options.label: Six
options.feedback: Wrong. Six seasons are recognized in some cultural calendars, like in India, not as the usual tropical pattern.

items.ok_line: Tropics often have wet and dry seasons.
items.ko_line: Wet and dry mark the year in most tropical areas.
items.exp_text: Because the Sun's tilt barely changes the sunlight in the tropics, temperature stays fairly steady. Instead, the rainy low-pressure belt moves north and south, so the year splits into a wet season and a dry season.

items.prompt: What is the angle of Earth's axial tilt?

options.label: About 10 degrees
options.feedback: Wrong. That is far less than Earth's actual tilt.

options.label: About 30 degrees
options.feedback: Wrong. The tilt is a bit less than this, closer to 23.4 degrees.

options.label: About 45 degrees
options.feedback: Wrong. That would make the poles lean much more than they do.

options.label: About 23.4 degrees
options.feedback: Correct. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up.

items.ko_line: Check the number—it's close to a quarter of a right angle.
items.exp_text: Earth's axis leans about 23.4 degrees away from being perpendicular to its orbit. That tilt is what makes different parts of Earth get more or less direct sunlight through the year.

items.prompt: What causes the seasons on Earth?

options.label: The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
options.feedback: Correct. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees, and as it orbits, different hemispheres lean toward or away from the Sun, creating the seasons.

options.label: The changing distance between Earth and the Sun
options.feedback: Not quite. Earth's distance to the Sun varies slightly, but this is not the cause of seasons; the tilt is.

options.label: The Sun's own brightness changing through the year
options.feedback: No. The Sun's brightness does not change with the seasons; Earth's tilt and orbit cause the seasonal pattern.

options.label: The Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans
options.feedback: That is other than the seasons. The Moon's gravity affects tides, not the yearly cycle of seasons.

items.ok_line: Earth's tilted axis gives different seasons as it orbits.
items.ko_line: Distance isn't the reason; the tilt drives seasons.
items.exp_text: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from vertical. As Earth travels around the Sun, this tilt makes one hemisphere lean toward the Sun while the other leans away, giving opposite seasons in the two hemispheres.

items.prompt: What is the approximate angle of Earth's axial tilt?

options.label: 10 degrees
options.feedback: That is too small. Earth's tilt is about 23.4 degrees, not 10.

options.label: 45 degrees
options.feedback: That is much larger than the actual tilt. The tilt is about 23.4 degrees, not 45.

options.label: 23.4 degrees
options.feedback: Correct. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from the perpendicular to its orbital plane.

options.label: 90 degrees
options.feedback: No. A 90-degree tilt would make the poles face the Sun directly, which is not the case. The tilt is about 23.4 degrees.

items.ok_line: Earth's axis leans by about 23.4 degrees.
items.ko_line: Check the number—it is near 23 degrees, not extremes.
items.exp_text: Earth's rotation axis is tilted by approximately 23.4 degrees relative to a line perpendicular to its orbital plane. This tilt is central to creating the seasons.

items.prompt: When it is summer in the Southern Hemisphere, what season is it in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.label: Summer
options.feedback: No. The two hemispheres are always opposite, so when one has summer the other has winter.

options.label: Spring
options.feedback: Not right. Opposite seasons mean summer in the south pairs with winter in the north, not spring.

options.label: Autumn
options.feedback: That is not correct. The seasons are opposite, so it would be winter, not autumn, in the Northern Hemisphere.

options.label: Winter
options.feedback: Correct. The Northern and Southern Hemispheres always have opposite seasons, so a southern summer means a northern winter.

items.ok_line: North and south are always opposite.
items.ko_line: When south has summer, north has winter.
items.exp_text: Because of Earth's axial tilt and its orbit, when one hemisphere leans toward the Sun the other leans away. So a southern summer is a northern winter, and vice versa.

items.prompt: What happens to day and night at the equinoxes?

options.label: Day and night are equally divided between the two hemispheres
options.feedback: Correct. At the equinoxes, the Sun is directly over the Equator, and both Poles are on the terminator, so day and night are about equal everywhere.

options.label: One hemisphere has all daylight
options.feedback: No. That would happen near solstices, not equinoxes. At equinoxes, day and night are balanced.

options.label: The night is longer than the day everywhere
options.feedback: Not right. At equinoxes, day and night are nearly equal in length, not one longer than the other everywhere.

options.label: Both hemispheres have a 24-hour day
options.feedback: No. That occurs only near the poles on specific dates near the solstices, not at equinoxes.

items.ok_line: At equinox, day and night balance out.
items.ko_line: Unequal days come near solstices, not equinoxes.
items.exp_text: An equinox happens when the Sun is directly over the Equator. Then the terminator line runs through both poles, so daylight and night are split nearly equally between the two hemispheres.

items.prompt: In which season does the Sun appear lower in the sky at noon in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.label: Summer
options.feedback: No. In summer, the Sun is higher in the sky at noon because that hemisphere tilts toward the Sun.

options.label: Spring
options.feedback: Not generally. Spring is a transition, but the Sun rises higher as summer approaches. The low noon Sun is characteristic of winter.

options.label: Winter
options.feedback: Correct. In winter, the Northern Hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so the Sun stays lower in the sky at noon, and its rays are more indirect.

options.label: Autumn
options.feedback: No. Autumn has a moderate noon Sun height, not the lowest. The lowest occurs in winter.

items.ok_line: Winter brings a low noon Sun.
items.ko_line: Summer has a high Sun; winter does not.
items.exp_text: Because of Earth's tilt, the noon Sun is high in the sky during summer and low in winter in the Northern Hemisphere. The low angle spreads sunlight over a larger area, making it weaker.

items.prompt: What is the main reason tropical regions have little seasonal temperature variation?

options.label: They are closer to the Sun
options.feedback: That is not correct. The distance to the Sun is not the cause; the tropics are not significantly closer in a way that matters.

options.label: Earth's tilt is not enough to greatly change the Sun's strength there
options.feedback: Correct. Earth's 23.4-degree tilt is too small to noticeably affect the strength of sunlight in the tropics, so temperatures stay fairly steady through the year.

options.label: They have no seasons at all because of the ocean
options.feedback: Not quite. The ocean moderates climate, but the key is that the Sun's rays stay strong all year at low latitudes.

options.label: They are always under clouds
options.feedback: No. Cloud cover is variable and not the primary reason for mild temperature swings in the tropics.

items.ok_line: The tilt barely changes tropical sunlight.
items.ko_line: The reason is the tilt's small effect near the equator.
items.exp_text: In tropical regions, the Sun is high in the sky all year because Earth's tilt of 23.4 degrees is too small to make a big difference there. Thus, temperature changes little between seasons, while rainfall can vary more.

items.prompt: In a temperate region, how many seasons are commonly recognized on a calendar?

options.label: Two
options.feedback: That is the model for many tropical regions, not for temperate ones. Temperate zones often use four seasons.

options.label: Three
options.feedback: Not typical. Three seasons are found in some tropical or historical calendars, but temperate regions usually have four.

options.label: Five
options.feedback: No. Five is not a common number here; the usual calendar model is four.

options.label: Four
options.feedback: Correct. Spring, summer, fall, and winter are the four seasons usually recognized in temperate and sub-polar regions.

items.ko_line: That count fits other regions or models.
items.exp_text: In temperate and sub-polar regions, four seasons—spring, summer, fall, and winter—are the standard based on the Gregorian calendar. Other regions and ecologists may use different numbers.
